slides.title: Twisted Pair Cable
slides.body:
Introduction
When two wires run parallel, both pick up the same external noise
Twisting them ensures that noise affects both wires equally, and at the receiver the noise cancels out (common-mode rejection)
The twisting is the key engineering trick
A twisted pair has two insulated copper wires twisted around each other

Cheap, easy to install
Used in office and home Ethernet

slides.title: Switching
slides.body: Switching

slides.title: Switching
slides.body:
Importance
Imagine a network of N devices, If every device needed a direct wire to every other device, 
The number of links would be N × (N − 1) / 2, For just 100 devices, that is 4,950 cables. For a million users, the number is impossible

slides.title: Switching
slides.body:
Solution - Switching
A small number of intermediate devices (switches, routers) sit in the middle, Each device connects only to a switch, and the switch decides where to forward the data
With N devices, only N links are needed

slides.title: Switching
slides.body:
Three Classic Switching Techniques
Circuit Switching
A dedicated path is set up before any data flows
Message Switching
The entire message is sent and stored at each intermediate node, then forwarded- no dedicated path
Packet Switching
the message is broken into small packets; each packet is forwarded independently
Each method makes different trade-offs in delay, bandwidth efficiency, and reliability

slides.title: Circuit Switching
slides.body:
Introduction
Device 1

Device 6 
The full bandwidth of every link on that path is reserved exclusively for this conversation, even when no data is flowing
Once the conversation ends, the circuit is torn down

slides.title: Circuit Switching
slides.body:
Three Phases of Session
Setup
1
A signaling message reserves a slot on every link from sender to receiver
Data Transfer
2
All data flows along the reserved path with constant, predictable delay
Teardown
3
when either side hangs up, the reservation is released at every switch

slides.title: Circuit Switching
slides.body:
Strengths
Guaranteed bandwidth
Predictable delay 
In-order delivery - perfect for voice calls

slides.title: Circuit Switching
slides.body:
Limitations
Wasteful - bandwidth is reserved even during silence in a phone call
Setup delay before any data can be sent
If any link on the reserved path fails, the entire call drops

slides.title: Circuit Switching
slides.body:
Real World Example
The old Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) used circuit switching
When someone made a call, the system reserved a path through the network, connecting the caller to the receiver

slides.title: Message Switching
slides.body:
Key Characteristics
No advance setup - data starts moving immediately
Each switch must store the entire message before forwarding it Switches need significant storage
Different messages may travel through completely different routes
If a link fails, the message can be re-routed at the next switch

slides.title: Message Switching
slides.body:
Limitations
Long delay - a switch cannot start forwarding until the entire message is received
Delay accumulates over hops
Not suitable for real-time data like voice or video
Switches need huge storage to buffer entire messages

slides.title: Packet Switching
slides.body:
Why Packet Switching Wins?
Pipelining
1
while one packet is being forwarded by Switch B, the next is being received by Switch A
Statistical multiplexing
2
Many flows share the same link efficiently, silent flows do not waste bandwidth
Robust
3
If a link fails, packets can be rerouted on the fly
Scalable
4
works equally well for two users or two billion

slides.title: Packet Switching
slides.body:
Trade-offs
Packets may arrive out of order - receiver reorders them using sequence numbers
Packets may be lost - handled by upper layers (TCP retransmits, UDP ignores)
Variable delay (jitter) - each packet may experience different queuing

slides.title: Performance Metrics
slides.body: Performance Metrics

slides.title: Performance Metrics
slides.body:
Important Terms
1
Bandwidth - The theoretical maximum:
The maximum data rate a link can carry, in bits per second
Determined by the physical medium and the encoding (Nyquist and Shannon)
Example: A Gigabit Ethernet link has a bandwidth of 1 Gbps

slides.title: Performance Metrics
slides.body:
2
Throughput - What is actually achieved
The actual data rate measured at any moment
Always less than or equal to bandwidth
Reduced by congestion, errors, and retransmissions
Example: On a 1 Gbps link, throughput during a busy office afternoon may be only 350 Mbps
Important Terms

slides.title: Performance Metrics
slides.body:
3
Goodput - Useful Throughput
The throughput of useful application data only -excluding headers and retransmissions
Always less than or equal to throughput, because every packet carries header overhead
Example: 350 Mbps throughput, after subtracting headers and retransmissions, may give 320 Mbps of actual file-download speed
Important Terms
The relationship is always: Goodput  ≤  Throughput  ≤  Bandwidth

Latency is the total time taken for a packet to travel from sender to receiver, It is the sum of four distinct components

A constant 50 ms latency is fine for voice, a latency that swings between 20 ms and 200 ms breaks voice and video calls even if the average is the same

slides.title: Real-World Performance - RTT and Bandwidth-Delay Product
slides.body:
RTT & BDP
Two derived metrics, RTT and Bandwidth-Delay Product, both of which directly affect TCP performance

slides.title: RTT
slides.body:
Round-Trip Time
The time for a packet to travel from sender to receiver and back, roughly 2 × one-way latency
Measured by tools like ping, TCP uses RTT to set timeouts
1 ms within a city
30 ms within a country
150 ms across continents (India to US East)
600 ms via satellite

slides.title: BDP
slides.body:
Bandwidth-Delay Product
Formula:  BDP  =  Bandwidth (bps)  ×  RTT (seconds)
Tells how many bits the network can hold in transit at any moment

slides.title: BDP
slides.body:
On a transcontinental high-speed link, BDP is huge - even a 10 Gbps link with 150 ms RTT has a BDP of 1.5 Gbits ≈ 187 MB
Modern operating systems use TCP window scaling to keep large BDPs full
Bandwidth-Delay Product

slides.title: Performance Metrics
slides.body:
Reading these Metrics in Real Life
A typical speedtest result shows three numbers:
Download / Upload speed
Ping (this is RTT)
Jitter (variation in RTT)
